prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I have moved from B046 to B036 and I want to give the reasons, not just the move. In round 1 I ranked the lattice clock last on overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and I told Kroll I may have been harsh. The exchange has since answered that objection on the physics. The new idea is the magic-wavelength lattice: the trap light shift cancels for the clock transition, so many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once with motional and Doppler shifts suppressed. Neither the comb, which is the readout ruler, nor single-ion control contains that step. It is what took neutral-atom clocks from the 10^-15 range to 10^-18, and it has been reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg in laboratories on several continents and compared over fibre links. My own field is superconducting circuits, so I rely on the atomic physicists here, Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson, on the physics, and I note that all three independently describe the same concept-plus-realisation structure. The credit also repairs what I could not repair for B046: two names, Katori for the concept and first lattice clocks, Ye for driving systematics and coherence to the record regime. A three-name cut from Zoller, Bloch, Greiner, Cirac, Esslinger and Jaksch leaves at least one arguably decisive person out, and nobody in round 1 showed me a way to avoid that. The chair's summary also shows B046 with one explicit supporter, me, so my own configuration was the least supported one on the table. That is not a reason by itself, but it does mean nobody else tested it, and the one member who commented on it (Pearce) rated the credit problem as decisive. I accept that this is a precision-measurement prize and that the 'another digit' charge has force; my answer is that going from a clock limited by Doppler and light shifts to one limited by blackbody radiation and gravitational redshift across millimetres is a change in what can be measured, and constants tests and relativistic geodesy follow from it.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to B036 remains lineage and boundary. The frequency comb (2005) and ion control (2012) are honoured, ion clocks (Al+) reached similar uncertainty, and PTB, NIST, SYRTE, RIKEN, Lemonde, Gill and Takamoto have close claims that two names cannot cover. The citation therefore has to be written around the lattice concept and the 10^-18 realisation and must not adjudicate lattice versus ion clocks. I would also leave Ye's many-body and spin-exchange work out of the citation, agreeing with Olsson, since it adds a second storyline; that is a drafting choice the committee should settle. The redefinition of the second has not happened and the prize should not rest on it. By leaving B046 I also give up the field with the widest reach into condensed matter and quantum information, and I still think quantum simulation will be rewarded in a later year once the Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram question is further along. For B022, I still think the pairing mechanism and Cao's absence from the three names are real obstacles, but they are the kind that time can reduce.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the magic-wavelength lattice, not timekeeping at large, is the distinct step, that the prize should be framed so it does not adjudicate lattice versus ion clocks, and that the committee should decide whether his Hall-laboratory stay requires recusal.
responses.response: This is what moved me. Your point that the comb is a readout tool while the lattice is the new content, and your refusal to claim lattice clocks beat ion clocks on merit, give a citation I can defend. On your recusal question, I would say a doctoral research stay in Hall's laboratory, with no documented tie to Katori or Ye, is a lineage connection and not a personal or collaborative one. I would treat it as disclosed, and I would not ask you to step back, but I would want it minuted. If the committee disagrees, the case should still stand on the other seven members, which is a reason to keep the discussion on the physics. I also thank you for your round-1 note on B046; I no longer press it, because the Cirac and Esslinger problem you accepted is the same one I could not solve.

responses.point: Lindroth says Katori's magic-wavelength trapping is a conceptual step that neither the comb nor ion control contains, that it enabled the move from 10^-15 to 10^-18 with many-atom statistics, and that the citation must be narrow so it does not read as a second metrology prize for the same achievement.
responses.response: I agree and I have adopted your wording of the conceptual step in my citation. In round 1 I told you the clock's conceptual novelty was narrower than lattice simulation; I now think that was wrong, since you and Kroll showed that the many-atom interrogation at a magic wavelength is a distinct idea with a measurable consequence. One difference remains. You would credit Ye's many-body and spin-exchange control, and I side with Olsson in leaving it out, because it ties the prize to a second line of work and invites the thorium nuclear-clock question that you yourself raised. If the committee prefers your wording, I would not object, so long as the name list stays at two.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps B022 first as a nature-led surprise preceded by a sharp prediction, notes broad top-three support, and says replication across many groups makes a 2026 prize defensible, with B036 as a fallback he would not oppose.
responses.response: I take the prediction-then-discovery pattern seriously and B022 stays in my alternatives. Our disagreement is about whether the open pairing mechanism matters. Mehlig argues the prize would rest on flat-band-driven correlated phases and not on a theory of superconductivity, and that is a fair reading. But the credit gap is not repaired by that argument: Cao is first author of the decisive 2018 papers and is outside the three names, and earlier moire band theorists are also left out. A three-name B022 prize therefore has the same kind of attribution weakness that made me abandon B046. Since you say you would not oppose B036, I would ask you to say whether you could vote for it as a final choice if B022's credit problem is judged unrepaired.

responses.point: Pearce argues that B046 is weaker than B036 on attribution because Cirac and Esslinger would be excluded, and says the answer to the 2005 and 2012 overlap must be argued explicitly and not assumed.
responses.response: You were right on the B046 attribution, and I have changed my configuration for that reason among others. On the overlap, I think it can be stated in two sentences: the comb is the ruler that reads the clock, and ion control concerns single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock interrogates many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength where the trap perturbation cancels. I would also share your caution that the PTB, NIST and SYRTE clocks and the ion programmes are close enough to make the wording exact. As chair you have also said the prize should not rest on the redefinition of the second, and I agree: the redefinition is a consequence of the result, not its justification.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the clocks far from his field, wants to know whether the magic-wavelength idea is the decisive conceptual step, and says he would take B036 as a serious configuration if Kroll and Lindroth showed that.
responses.response: I am outside atomic metrology as well, so I can only report what I find persuasive in the exchange: Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce all identify the same step, and Mehlig and Danielsson, who disfavour B036, do not dispute it. Their objection is about whether a precision advance should count, not about whether the idea is new. I would ask you to consider whether that satisfies the condition you set in round 1.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a distinct invention from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I am relying on atomic physicists for this and cannot independently settle priority between Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Gill and others.
Whether Ye's many-body and spin-exchange work belongs in the citation, and whether two names are enough given PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN claims.
Whether the committee, on balance, regards a precision-measurement invention as outweighing a younger field-opening discovery such as B022 once the credit gap for Cao is weighed.

Whether quantum simulation (B046) is a discovery rather than a method, and whether any three of Zoller, Bloch, Greiner, Cirac, Esslinger and Jaksch could be chosen without decisive injustice; I could not settle this and have set it aside.
statement.conflict_note: My earlier disclosure stands. I direct WACQT at Chalmers and work on circuit and waveguide QED, so I would flag a recusal issue on B044 and on any quantum-computing hardware candidate; my documented ties are to Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and to frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum, and none of them is among the credited names of B036, B046 or B022. For my final position, B036 (Katori and Ye), no specific conflict is apparent from my profile. B044 is no longer in my configuration or alternatives, so I do not need to step back from any part of it.
